title: Why OSPF Matters
body: OSPF is the routing protocol most enterprise networks run internally. Every question in this module is really asking one thing: does a router have a complete, identical picture of the network before it calculates paths? Get that mental model right and the rest — states, elections, timers — falls into place.
keyPoints: OSPF is classless and link-state — every router builds a full topology map, not just a list of routes.
It's the most heavily tested routing protocol in the ENSA exam.

title: The Link-State Big Picture
body: Forget the acronyms for a second. Every link-state protocol follows the same five-step recipe. OSPF just gives each step a name and a packet type.
keyPoints: The link-state database (LSDB) ends up identical on every router in an area — only the resulting routing table differs per router.
SPF (Dijkstra) runs locally on each router against its own copy of that shared database.

title: Neighbor States — the Handshake
body: Two OSPF routers don't become full neighbors instantly. They climb a ladder of states, and exam questions love to ask which state a symptom points to.
keyPoints: DR/BDR election happens during Two-Way — not before, not after.
In ExStart, the router with the higher Router ID becomes master and sends the first DBD.
Only DR and BDR reach Full with every neighbor; two DROTHERs only reach Two-Way with each other.

title: DR/BDR Election on a Multiaccess Segment
body: On a shared segment (like a switch), every router doesn't need to peer with every other router — that would be n(n-1)/2 adjacencies. Instead, one Designated Router and one Backup Designated Router become the hub everyone else talks to.
keyPoints: Election tiebreak order: highest OSPF interface priority (0–255, 0 = never eligible), then highest Router ID.
DROTHERs send updates to the DR/BDR via multicast 224.0.0.6; the DR/BDR floods to everyone via 224.0.0.5.
Point-to-point links never elect a DR/BDR — only two routers can ever exist on that segment.

title: Router ID Selection Order
body: Before any of this can happen, every router needs a unique 32-bit Router ID. OSPF picks it in a strict order — and exam questions test exactly this order.

steps.label: Highest IP on any loopback interface
Highest IP on any active physical interface

keyPoints: A manually set router-id always wins, even over a higher loopback address.
Loopback interfaces are preferred over physical ones because they never go down — a stable Router ID means a stable OSPF process.

title: The Five OSPF Packet Types
body: Every OSPF conversation is built from five packet types. Knowing which one does what turns a wall of acronyms into a simple story: say hello, describe what you have, ask for what's missing, send it, confirm you got it.
keyPoints: Hello packets are sent every 10 seconds by default on broadcast/point-to-point links; the Dead interval is always 4x Hello.
LSU (Type 4) is what actually carries the LSAs — DBD (Type 2) is just a table of contents.

title: Watch Out For…
body: The two traps that catch people who understand OSPF conceptually but rush the questions.
keyPoints: "Two-Way" is not the final state — students often stop reading here. Full adjacency (databases synchronized) is what matters for routing.
A DROTHER-to-DROTHER relationship staying at Two-Way is normal, not a fault — they don't need each other's full database.
Default OSPF cost = reference bandwidth ÷ interface bandwidth. Gigabit and FastEthernet both hit the cost-1 floor unless you raise the reference bandwidth with auto-cost.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You've got the shape of single-area OSPF: the link-state process, the neighbor state ladder, DR/BDR election, Router ID selection, and the five packet types. That's exactly what this module's questions test.
keyPoints: OSPF's default administrative distance is 110.
The LSDB is identical per area; the neighbor table and routing table are unique per router.
An ASBR connects the OSPF domain to an external network and can inject a default route.
